title: Does exposure to air pollution increase the risk of dying from the coronavirus (COVID-19)?
meta_description: Our analysis measures the link between long-term exposure to dirty air and COVID-19 deaths in England.

breadcrumb.text: Does exposure to air pollution increase the risk of dying from the coronavirus (COVID-19)?

lede: Our analysis measures the link between long-term exposure to dirty air and COVID-19 deaths in England.

body.text: 13 August 2020

The coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic has led to a big drop in pollution levels – global carbon emissions per day were [up to 17% lower than normal](https://www.carbonbrief.org/daily-global-co2-emissions-cut-to-2006-levels-during-height-of-coronavirus-crisis) at one stage in early April, returning to levels last seen in 2006.
However, some studies have suggested that long-term exposure to air pollution before the pandemic is associated with severe symptoms from COVID-19 and a greater risk of death.

Studies in the United States (US), Northern Italy and the Netherlands all found that a small increase in pollution exposure raises the number of COVID-19 deaths, with the most recent study in the Netherlands pointing to a rise in the death rate of up to 21%.

Our analysis examines the [impact of long-term exposure to air pollution on COVID-19 deaths in England](http://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/environmentalaccounts/methodologies/coronaviruscovid19relatedmortalityratesandtheeffectsofairpollutioninengland), with results pointing to a smaller effect than previous studies.

body.h2: What links pollution exposure and COVID-19 deaths?
body.text: Consistent exposure to air pollution is a known cause of breathing difficulties and other long-term conditions in the lungs and the heart.

body.h2: What links pollution exposure and COVID-19 deaths?
body.text: Our data show that more than one-third (35%) of deaths involving COVID-19 in England up to the end of June had a respiratory or cardiovascular disease as the main pre-existing health condition.

body.h2: What links pollution exposure and COVID-19 deaths?
body.text: We have published [detailed analysis](http://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/environmentalaccounts/methodologies/coronaviruscovid19relatedmortalityratesandtheeffectsofairpollutioninengland) showing that deaths involving COVID-19 were more common in highly polluted areas, particularly early in the pandemic.

body.h2: What links pollution exposure and COVID-19 deaths?
body.text: However, the correlation between pollution and mortality fell as deaths rose and lockdown was introduced, before levelling off in early May.

body.h2: What links pollution exposure and COVID-19 deaths?
body.text: The link between early COVID-19 deaths and exposure to dirty air was partly down to the outbreak in London (where pollution levels are generally higher than the rest of the country).

body.h2: What links pollution exposure and COVID-19 deaths?
body.text: Up to the week when lockdown began (week ending 27 March 2020), 45% of COVID-19 deaths in England had occurred in the capital. By the week ending 12 June (cut-off date for this analysis), this had fallen to 18%.

body.h2: What links pollution exposure and COVID-19 deaths?
body.text: As the virus spread across the country and deaths became more evenly distributed, the correlation between air pollution exposure and COVID-19 mortality decreased.

body.h2: What links pollution exposure and COVID-19 deaths?
body.text: Our analysis includes 46,471 deaths involving COVID-19 among usual residents of England between 7 March 2020 and 12 June 2020, registered by 22 June 2020.

body.h2: What links pollution exposure and COVID-19 deaths?
body.text: We considered exposure to ozone, fine particulate matter (known as PM2.5), and nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and NOx. We did not account for changes in pollution levels since the pandemic began.

body.h2: The effects of long-term exposure to air pollution on COVID-19 deaths appear smaller than reported in previous studies
body.text: While death rates have generally been higher in polluted areas, this on its own does not establish pollution exposure as a cause of COVID-19 deaths.

body.h2: The effects of long-term exposure to air pollution on COVID-19 deaths appear smaller than reported in previous studies
body.text: To isolate the impact of air pollution, we developed a statistical model controlling for factors such as levels of deprivation, population density, public health (such as smoking rates) and pre-existing health conditions. This enables us to compare deaths among populations of similar health from the same sort of area, with the main difference being long-term exposure to air pollution.

body.h2: The effects of long-term exposure to air pollution on COVID-19 deaths appear smaller than reported in previous studies
body.text: We also controlled for ethnicity, thereby comparing deaths among populations with similar levels of ethnic diversity.

body.h2: The effects of long-term exposure to air pollution on COVID-19 deaths appear smaller than reported in previous studies
body.text: Our [previous analysis](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/articles/coronaviruscovid19relateddeathsbyethnicgroupenglandandwales/2march2020to15may2020) suggests that a range of structural differences are resulting in higher COVID-19 death rates among people of Black, Asian and Minority Ethnicity (BAME). Air pollution exposure could be a contributing factor if it causes COVID-19 deaths, with the BAME population more likely than those of White ethnicity to live in inner city areas (that are more polluted).

body.text: Ultimately, our analysis is inconclusive.

body.h2: The effects of long-term exposure to air pollution on COVID-19 deaths appear smaller than reported in previous studies
body.h4: Ethnicity is strongly correlated with pollution exposure, with ethnic minorities more likely to live in polluted areas
body.h5: Percentage of the population of Black, Asian and Minority Ethnicity (BAME) compared with average 10-year exposure to NO2, selected areas in England
body.text: Without controlling for ethnicity, we find that long-term exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) could increase the risk of contracting and dying from COVID-19 by up to 7% (comparable with results from a [US study](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.04.05.20054502v2)).

body.h2: The effects of long-term exposure to air pollution on COVID-19 deaths appear smaller than reported in previous studies
body.h4: Ethnicity is strongly correlated with pollution exposure, with ethnic minorities more likely to live in polluted areas
body.h5: Percentage of the population of Black, Asian and Minority Ethnicity (BAME) compared with average 10-year exposure to NO2, selected areas in England
body.text: However, when controlling for ethnicity, air pollution exposure has no statistically significant impact on COVID-19 deaths.

body.h2: The effects of long-term exposure to air pollution on COVID-19 deaths appear smaller than reported in previous studies
body.h4: Ethnicity is strongly correlated with pollution exposure, with ethnic minorities more likely to live in polluted areas
body.h5: Percentage of the population of Black, Asian and Minority Ethnicity (BAME) compared with average 10-year exposure to NO2, selected areas in England
body.text: As air pollution is just one of many factors that could be driving disproportionate outcomes for minority ethnic groups, the increased risk of dying from COVID-19 (found when ethnicity is not controlled for) is likely to be an overestimate of the true effect.

body.text: A [recent study of 400 COVID-19 patients admitted to a Birmingham hospital](https://www.researchsquare.com/article/rs-35617/v1) said that BAME patients were “more likely to be admitted from regions of highest air pollution, housing quality and household overcrowding deprivation”.

body.text: [Our approach in this study](http://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/environmentalaccounts/methodologies/coronaviruscovid19relatedmortalityratesandtheeffectsofairpollutioninengland) was not sufficient to pull all these factors apart. Achieving this is likely to require highly detailed individual-based modelling.

body.h2: The effects of long-term exposure to air pollution on COVID-19 deaths appear smaller than reported in previous studies
body.h4: Ethnicity is strongly correlated with pollution exposure, with ethnic minorities more likely to live in polluted areas
body.h5: Percentage of the population of Black, Asian and Minority Ethnicity (BAME) compared with average 10-year exposure to NO2, selected areas in England
body.text: In this study, we have only been able to examine air quality and COVID-19 deaths at the population level, based on the availability of existing data. At this level, we have to make assumptions such as consistent exposure to pollution across a 1km grid square. In reality, exposure could vary from one end of a street to another, and individual exposure is affected by where someone works as well as where they live.

body.h2: The effects of long-term exposure to air pollution on COVID-19 deaths appear smaller than reported in previous studies
body.h4: Ethnicity is strongly correlated with pollution exposure, with ethnic minorities more likely to live in polluted areas
body.h5: Percentage of the population of Black, Asian and Minority Ethnicity (BAME) compared with average 10-year exposure to NO2, selected areas in England
body.text: To disentangle factors such as pollution and ethnicity, and their contribution to COVID-19 mortality, we would need to identify detailed characteristics of the individuals who have died from COVID-19. While we hope to publish this kind of analysis in future, the data and modelling required take much longer to put together.
